examples: "Shall we meet at eight?" "OK."
OK, I'll do it right now.
note: Colloquial and extremely common in Spain. In Mexico more often “okey”.

examples: The party was really cool.
Your new house is great.
note: Colloquial; it does not change form: un plan guay, una casa guay.

examples: That lad plays the guitar really well.
The kids play football in the square.
note: Colloquial. Chavala = girl.

examples: I'm meeting my mates on Saturday.
He's a colleague from work.
note: Colloquial, also for women: la colega. In Mexico more often “amigo”.

examples: There were loads of people at the concert.
I have heaps of things to do.
note: Colloquial: un mogollón de = a huge amount of.

examples: Come on, we're going to be late!
Right then, see you later.
note: Colloquial: encouragement, agreement or a goodbye.

examples: Wow! I didn't know you lived here.
Come on, help me with this.
note: A colloquial exclamation of surprise or a gentle request.

examples: What a surprise!
Oh dear, I forgot my phone!
note: An exclamation of surprise, annoyance or admiration.

examples: What amazing views!
My sister ran a marathon. That's amazing!
note: Colloquial; admiration or astonishment.

examples: I'm wrecked after the trip.
After the match we were all exhausted.
note: Colloquial; “hecho” agrees with the person: hecha polvo, hechos polvo.

examples: Your sister is very nice.
You have very nice neighbours.
note: Colloquial: nice, likeable. In Mexico more often “simpático”.

examples: What a cool flat you have!
You're wearing a really nice T-shirt.
note: Colloquial. Careful: about a person it can also mean “cocky, cheeky”.

examples: The hotel was a bit shabby.
It's a shabby bar, but the food is good.
note: Colloquial; it does not change with gender.

examples: My cousin is a bit posh.
He goes to a very posh school.
note: Colloquial, a little mocking: rich and showy.

examples: Tomorrow I have a lot of work.
I'm looking for a job.
note: Colloquial. Verb: currar. In Mexico “chamba”.

examples: I haven't got the money for the trip.
I love pasta with tomato.
note: Colloquially “money”. In Mexico “lana”.

examples: We went partying, in a relaxed kind of way.
He spoke to me in a rude kind of way.
note: Colloquial, mostly young people; similar to “like”.

examples: We order a few tapas and a beer.
This ham tapa is delicious.
note: In some cities (e.g. Granada) you get a free tapa with your drink.

examples: A small beer, please.
We have a few beers after work.
note: In Spain you order a beer as “una caña”. Careful: cana = grey hair.

examples: I'd like a ham sandwich.
My favourite sandwich is the omelette one.
note: A filled baguette, a typical lunch or snack. In Mexico “torta”.

examples: My grandmother's potato omelette is the best.
We order a potato omelette to share.
note: The most typical Spanish dish: eggs, potatoes and sometimes onion.

examples: In summer we have gazpacho.
Gazpacho is served cold.
note: A cold soup made of tomatoes, cucumber and peppers.

examples: The ham croquettes are delicious.
My mother makes very good croquettes.
For breakfast we have chocolate with churros.
The churros are freshly made.
note: Traditionally with thick hot chocolate.

examples: In summer we drink a lot of sangria.
A jug of sangria to share?
note: Wine with fruit and ice.

examples: On Sundays we have a vermouth before lunch.
A vermouth with an olive, please.
note: “Tomar el vermú” is a Sunday aperitif before lunch.

examples: For breakfast I have coffee with a magdalena.
My grandmother makes lemon magdalenas.
This peach is very sweet.
In summer we eat lots of peaches.
note: In Mexico “durazno”.

examples: Do you want peanuts with your beer?
I'm allergic to peanuts.
note: In Mexico “cacahuate”.

examples: I don't like peas.
Give me a little rice with peas.
note: In Mexico “chícharo”.

examples: To start, green beans with ham.
Green beans are boiled for ten minutes.
note: In Mexico “ejote”.

examples: Beans with chorizo is a typical dish.
My grandmother makes really good beans.
note: Dried white beans; in Mexico “frijoles”.

examples: The milk is in the fridge.
The fridge needs cleaning.
note: In Mexico “refrigerador” or “refri”.

examples: The set menu costs twelve euros.
In this bar the set menu includes dessert.
note: A lunch set (starter, main, dessert, drink) at a fixed price; in Mexico “comida corrida”.

examples: The bathroom tap is dripping.
Turn off the tap, please.
note: In Mexico “llave”.

examples: Mop the kitchen floor.
The mop is on the balcony.
note: In Mexico “trapeador”.

examples: Do you have a lighter?
I lost my lighter.
note: In Mexico “encendedor”.

examples: Where is the toilet?
The house has two toilets and a bathroom.
note: A small toilet without a bath; in public places “los aseos”.

examples: He lives in a penthouse with a terrace.
Penthouses are usually expensive.
note: A flat on the top floor, often with a terrace.

examples: I'll wait for you at the entrance.
The entrance is locked.
note: The shared entrance of an apartment building.

examples: There is a letter in the mailbox.
The mailbox is full of junk mail.
We live in a housing development with a pool.
The development is on the outskirts.
note: A residential complex of houses or flats, often with a shared pool; in Mexico “fraccionamiento”.

examples: They have a cottage in the mountains.
We rent a villa for the summer.
note: A detached house, villa or cottage; also spelled “chalet”.

examples: The rent for the flat is very expensive.
I pay the rent on the first.
note: In Mexico “renta”.

examples: It's cold today, put on a jumper.
This jumper is made of wool.
note: In Mexico “suéter”.

examples: I'm wearing blue jeans.
These jeans are too big for me.
note: Always plural. In Mexico “pantalones de mezclilla” or “jeans”.

examples: I forgot my swimming trunks at home.
I need new swimming trunks.
note: In Mexico “traje de baño”.

examples: I go to the gym in a tracksuit.
I put on my tracksuit and went running.
note: In Mexico “ropa deportiva”.

examples: He is wearing a blue blazer for the interview.
This blazer suits you very well.
note: In Mexico “saco” or “blazer”.

examples: Put your jacket on, it's windy.
I bought a leather jacket.
note: A short jacket (leather, denim…).

examples: I wear trainers for walking.
These trainers are very comfortable.
note: “Zapatillas de casa” = slippers. In Mexico “tenis”.

examples: There is a car park near the museum.
I can't find a parking space.
note: In Mexico “estacionamiento”.

examples: The town hall is in the square.
I went to the town hall to ask for a permit.
note: In Mexico “palacio municipal”.

examples: I buy stamps at the tobacconist's.
The tobacconist's opens at nine.
note: A state-licensed shop selling tobacco, stamps and transport tickets.

examples: I buy the newspaper at the newsstand.
The kiosk on the corner sells magazines.
I go to work by commuter train.
The commuter train leaves every fifteen minutes.
note: RENFE commuter trains around big cities; used in the plural.

examples: We take the dual carriageway to Valencia.
The autovía is free, the autopista is not.
note: A toll-free fast road; an “autopista” is a toll motorway.

examples: Show me your boarding pass, please.
I lost my boarding pass.
note: In Mexico “pase de abordar”.

examples: We left our suitcases in the left-luggage office.
The station left-luggage office closes at ten.
We have dinner on a terrace.
In summer the terraces are full.
note: Outdoor seating in front of a bar is part of daily life in Spain.

examples: My brother studies at secondary school.
My secondary school was near home.
note: Secondary school for ages 12–18; in Mexico “secundaria” and “preparatoria”.

examples: I study a lot for the university entrance exam.
My sister got a good mark in the entrance exam.
note: The national exam after secondary school that decides university admission (officially EBAU/PAU).

examples: I got a pass in maths.
A pass is good enough for me.
note: Marks: suspenso (0–4.9), aprobado (5), notable (7), sobresaliente (9–10).

examples: I have a fail in English.
A fail is not the end of the world.
I got a top mark in history.
You need a top mark for the scholarship.
note: The top mark (9–10).

examples: Unemployment has fallen this year.
I have been unemployed since March.
note: “Estar en el paro” = to be unemployed.

examples: My father is self-employed.
The self-employed pay a monthly fee.
note: Woman: la autónoma.

examples: My cousin is preparing the exam to become a teacher.
She passed the exam and is now a civil servant.
note: A demanding competitive exam for public service (teacher, judge…). Used in the plural.

examples: There is no socket nearby.
He got the job through connections.
note: Colloquially: conseguir algo por enchufe = to get something through connections.

examples: On New Year's Eve we eat twelve grapes.
We spend New Year's Eve with the family.
note: At midnight you eat one grape at each chime of the bells.

examples: What are you doing this weekend?
At the weekend we are going to the beach.
note: Colloquial short form of “fin de semana”.

examples: After lunch I take a siesta.
In summer the siesta is sacred.
